description: 2gbram, yazılım geliştirme, yapay zekâ, veri analizi ve 3D görselleştirme alanlarında deneyime sahip, yenilikçi teknolojiler üretmeye odaklanan bir ekiptir. Farklı disiplinlerdeki teknik bilgi birikimimizi birleştirerek gerçek problemlere yaratıcı ve uygulanabilir çözümler geliştirmeyi hedefliyoruz. NASA Space Apps Challenge kapsamında Ay İniş Alanı Navigatörü projesiyle bilimsel verileri, mühendislik yaklaşımlarını ve modern yazılım teknolojilerini bir araya getirmeyi amaçlıyoruz.
summary:
Team 2gbram built a web prototype that combines classical simulation and quantum optimization to plan landings and communications near the Moon’s south pole.

The classical component uses NASA lunar elevation data and JPL ephemerides to compare candidate landing sites by terrain, sunlight, and direct visibility of Earth. If an obstacle blocks the original target during a simulated landing, the system evaluates backup sites and updates the plan when a candidate passes the landing checks.

The quantum component explores how to select communication relays when direct visibility of Earth is limited. We formulated the choice of two relay orbits from four candidates as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. We ran a four-qubit Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) circuit in simulation and on Rigetti quantum hardware. The hardware returned the same optimal relay pair as the classical benchmark in 51 of 256 measurements.

The prototype brings landing site selection, mission timing, and communication planning into a single workflow.
details:
What we built

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web prototype for planning missions near the Moon’s south pole. It helps users compare landing sites and dates, examine sunlight and Earth visibility, and test how a mission plan could change if an obstacle blocks the original landing target. It also lets users explore whether orbital relays could improve modeled communication coverage when direct visibility of Earth is limited.

NASA data and external APIs

  • NASA JPL Horizons API: We retrieve the positions of the Sun and Earth as seen from selected lunar sites over a user-defined time window. We compare their apparent elevations with the local terrain horizon to estimate when the Sun is visible and when the site has a direct line of sight to Earth. We also use Horizons data to estimate when the Moon is above the minimum elevation at selected Deep Space Network stations.
  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data: We use lunar elevation data at approximately 80 meters per grid cell to calculate local slopes and terrain horizons. Nearby ridges can block sunlight or the view of Earth even when the Sun or Earth is above the ideal geometric horizon.
  • NASA Deep Space Network documentation: We use station coordinates for Goldstone, Canberra, and Madrid to estimate geometric communication windows. These estimates do not include antenna scheduling or a radio link budget.
  • NASA JPL Three-Body Periodic Orbits API: We retrieve initial conditions for candidate halo orbits around the Earth–Moon L2 point. We propagate these orbits classically using the circular restricted three-body problem model, then estimate relay coverage and communication gaps for selected lunar sites.

The digital twin and mission simulations

Our digital twin is a simulation of the lunar mission environment. It combines real terrain and astronomical data with modeled spacecraft behavior. Users can select a site and time window, inspect how visibility changes over time, and compare scenarios using measures such as sunlight duration, the longest continuous period of darkness, and Earth visibility.

For example, we compared two 24-hour windows at the same Malapert site. Moving the start date from November 4 to November 6 increased the time when the Sun was at least partially visible by 19.1 hours. Earth visibility duration stayed the same. This shows why choosing a date can change the solar power outlook even when the landing site and the duration of Earth visibility remain fixed.

We also simulated an obstacle appearing at the original landing target. The original plan failed the landing checks. The replanning module evaluated backup sites and switched to a candidate that passed those checks. If no candidate passes, the system reports that it found no valid continuation plan. The flight and obstacle were simulated on real lunar terrain.

How the hybrid classical and quantum system works

The classical layer prepares the data, computes orbital geometry and relay coverage, and defines the constraints that a relay selection must meet. The quantum layer tackles a discrete decision within that workflow: which two relay orbits should we select from four candidates? We encoded the decision as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and implemented a four-qubit, single-layer Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) circuit in Qiskit.

We compared the circuit’s output with an exhaustive classical search on the same problem. An independent classical check evaluated the sampled selections against the original coverage constraints, and we kept invalid samples in the reported results.

  • Local QAOA simulation: 208 of 256 samples met the constraints, including 55 that matched the classical optimum.
  • Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q hardware via OpenQuantum: 129 of 256 samples met the constraints, including 51 that matched the classical optimum.

This experiment demonstrates how a quantum circuit can propose relay selections within a mission planning workflow and how classical checks can validate its output. The four-candidate case is small enough to solve by exhaustive search, so these results do not establish a quantum speed or performance advantage.

Implementation and intended impact

We built the interactive interface with React and TypeScript, the analysis services with Python and FastAPI, and the background data pipeline with RabbitMQ. Docker Compose runs the services together, and Qiskit supports the quantum experiments. The data pipeline caches retrieved data and retains source information so analyses can be traced back to their inputs.

The prototype helps students, researchers, and mission design teams see how landing site, timing, terrain, and communications affect one another. By making the inputs, constraints, and results visible, it gives users a way to explain why one plan works better than another under the modeled conditions and to test what changes when those conditions change.
